assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2018 observation of correlated-insulator and superconducting states at the magic angle opened a new door: a tunable platform for strongly correlated physics in a single, cleanly controlled material. It is an original experiment with a clear theoretical precursor, and the field it launched is large and still growing.
assessment.attribution: Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle in 2011, so a theory-plus-experiment prize is natural and fits three names. Other experimental groups (e.g. Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov) contributed important follow-up, and I would want the record on who was first at each sub-result reviewed.
assessment.maturity: Replicated by many independent groups across devices and techniques, including scanning probes and transport. The interpretation of the superconducting pairing remains unsettled, but the existence of the phenomena is solid. Recognition is timely, about eight years after discovery.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is not settled, so the prize motivation should rest on the observation and the flat-band platform.
Whether the original experiment should be recognised alone, with theory, or with other early experimental groups.
I rely on my own recollection of the chronology and have not verified it here.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Correcting spherical aberration of electron lenses overcame a limit on resolution that stood since Scherzer's 1936 theorem. It brought routine sub-angstrom imaging and spectroscopy of atoms in materials, an instrument invention that opened doors across physics, chemistry and materials science. This is the kind of enabling tool the prize has recognised before.
assessment.attribution: Rose (design theory), Haider (implementation in TEM, with Rose and others) and Urban (Juelich, applied it in practice) are a coherent trio. Krivanek's independent STEM corrector and Dellby's contribution are not among the credited names, which is an unresolved allocation of credit I would need to see handled carefully. As a microscopist in this field I should be mindful of my own proximity to this area and rely on the documented record.
assessment.maturity: Commercially deployed for over two decades and used in thousands of publications, so the impact and independent confirmation are very strong. Recognition is not premature.
uncertainties: Krivanek, Dellby and others made parallel STEM corrector contributions that the credited names do not cover.
Which of the three credited names did the original instrument demonstration versus the theory.
My own field proximity may bias my reading of the relative importance.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in 1995 was the original experiment that made magnetic tunnel junctions practical. MgO junctions with coherent tunnelling then produced large effects, enabling read heads and MRAM. It is a clean experimental discovery with clear benefit and technological reach.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995, and Parkin and the Yuasa/Djayaprawira line established large MgO TMR in 2004. The credited trio is plausible, but Yuasa and Djayaprawira (not credited) did much of the MgO work, and the prize would be a split between two discoveries.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed in many laboratories and in industrial products, so very mature. The 2007 prize for GMR is a close relative, which raises the question of whether this is sufficiently distinct.
uncertainties: Overlap in scientific theme with the 2007 GMR prize.
Credit for MgO coherent tunnelling beyond the credited names.
Whether the TMR discovery and the MgO result should be treated as a single prize motivation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, trapped many atoms in a lattice without perturbing the clock transition and reached 10^-18 stability. It enables tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. Experimentally verified and broadly useful.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the original proposal and first demonstration; Ye's group drove the precision to the extreme with Sr lattice clocks. Two laureates fit well and the credited list is already the right size. Hall and Haensch were recognised in 2005 for the comb, so a clear separation exists. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto) are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Several independent clocks agree at the 10^-18 level, and the redefinition of the second is under discussion. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether single-ion clocks and the Al+ work by Wineland, Rosenband and others make the field attribution broader than the credited pair.
Credit split between proposal and precision realisation.
Redefinition of the second is not yet complete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube opened neutrino astronomy by observing a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos in 2013, evidence for TXS 0506+056, and the Galactic plane. It is an instrument that opens a door onto a universe that could not be seen before, with confirmed observations and lasting significance.
assessment.attribution: Halzen led the concept and the collaboration, and Spiering has a long record in neutrino telescopes, including Baikal and AMANDA. Large-collaboration attribution is difficult, and the Baikal-GVD and ANTARES/KM3NeT communities and the AMANDA pioneers, such as Learned and Roberts for DUMAND, are not in the credited list.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is well established and the Galactic and source evidence has appeared in the past few years. Source identification is still developing, so there is some risk of premature recognition.
uncertainties: Attribution within a collaboration of hundreds, with earlier pioneers not credited.
Sources of the diffuse flux remain largely unidentified.
Whether the prize should wait for stronger source associations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson by ATLAS and CMS completed the Standard Model in an experiment of historic scale. It is a verified discovery of fundamental importance, and the 2013 prize recognised the theory.
assessment.attribution: The experimental credit is the hardest part. Thousands of collaborators contributed, and the three names are the founding spokespersons and proposers rather than those who made the decisive measurement. The rules on at most three laureates and individuals do not map well, and I would want a clear argument on who did the original work rather than directing the instrument.
assessment.maturity: Two independent experiments confirm the result and the couplings have been measured steadily since. The finding is very mature.
uncertainties: Whether spokespersons and project leaders are the right individuals to name.
The statutes limit the prize to three persons, which is a poor fit for a collaboration discovery.
The prize for the theory in 2013 already recognised the central idea.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators created a new class of materials. The theory by Kane and Mele (2005) and the 2007 HgTe experiment by Molenkamp's group established the topic, and the field has driven much work on spin transport and topological matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the theory, and Molenkamp's group, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's prediction, did the original quantum spin Hall observation. Zhang is deceased, and Bernevig and Hughes are not credited. Experimental discoveries of 3D topological insulators (Hasan, Cava, Hsieh) are a further complication. The attribution is distributed across several communities.
assessment.maturity: The HgTe experiment is well confirmed and the 3D materials are heavily studied. Applications are not yet established, which weighs on the benefit criterion.
uncertainties: Competing credit among Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Hasan and others.
Whether a prize is better for the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or for 3D topological insulators.
Practical benefit not yet demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum anomalous Hall effect observed in 2013 in a magnetic topological insulator gave quantised Hall resistance with no external magnetic field. It is an original experimental realisation of a long-sought effect with relevance to dissipationless transport and metrology.
assessment.attribution: Xue's group did the experiment, and Fang and Dai made the specific theoretical proposal in 2010. The first author of the experiment, Cui-Zu Chang, is not on the credited list, and Haldane's earlier 1988 model is background credit. The allocation between experiment and theory remains open.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced in several laboratories, but the quantisation temperature remains very low, so applications are not yet at hand. The recognition could be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Credit for Chang and others on the experimental team.
Low operating temperature limits practical impact so far.
Relationship to the Haldane model and the topological insulator body of work.
